questions.stem: Which patients require appropriate postanesthesia management under ASA postanesthesia standards? (Select 3)
options: A patient given a surgeon-placed local without anesthesia team care
A patient who had an anesthesia consult without a procedure
A patient after monitored anesthesia care
A patient after a peripheral nerve block alone
A patient seen in preop who canceled before any anesthetic
questions.explanation: Standard I covers all patients who received general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or MAC. Patients who received no anesthetic from the anesthesia team aren't covered by this standard.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: After a lap chole, who must accompany the patient to PACU?
options: An anesthesia team member who knows the patient
A transport aide with a portable monitor and oxygen
questions.explanation: Standard II requires transport accompanied by an anesthesia care team member knowledgeable about the patient, who evaluates and treats the patient during transport. Other staff don't meet the standard.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: During transport to PACU, a patient's SpO2 drifts to 90% on room air. Which standard applies MOST directly?
options: Physician responsibility for PACU discharge decisions
Continual evaluation and treatment en route
questions.explanation: Standard II requires the patient to be continually evaluated and treated during transport with monitoring and support appropriate to the condition, so oxygen and airway support should already be in place. The other standards apply on arrival, in PACU, or at discharge.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: On PACU arrival, what does ASA Standard III require?
options: Re-evaluation and verbal report to the nurse
Written orders without a verbal report
Report to any available PACU staff member on arrival
questions.explanation: Standard III requires re-evaluation on arrival and a verbal report from the accompanying anesthesia team member to the responsible PACU nurse. Written orders alone or report to anyone available don't meet it.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which ASA postanesthesia standard requires the patient's condition to be evaluated continually in PACU?
questions.explanation: Standard IV requires continual evaluation in PACU. Standard II covers transport, Standard III arrival and report, and Standard V discharge.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Under ASA Standard V, who is responsible for discharging a patient from PACU?
options: A physician, though criteria may guide it
The anesthesia provider who did the case, in person
questions.explanation: Standard V makes a physician responsible for discharge; departments may use approved discharge criteria applied by nurses. Many institutions require anesthesia evaluation before discharge for higher-risk patients. A charge nurse alone isn't responsible under the standard.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: ASA 2 patient meets all PACU discharge criteria after knee arthroscopy. Under a typical criteria-based policy, what is MOST appropriate?
options: The surgeon signs a separate PACU discharge order
The patient waits for a physician in person
The anesthesia provider examines the patient first
questions.explanation: Healthier patients (often ASA 1–2) can usually be discharged by the PACU nurse using department-approved criteria. Higher-risk patients, often ASA 3–4, may need an anesthesia provider's evaluation and order.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: ASA 4 patient after a hip replacement meets standard PACU scoring criteria. Under a typical policy, what is MOST appropriate before discharge from PACU?
options: Nurse discharge once the Aldrete score reaches 7
questions.explanation: Higher-risk patients, typically ASA 3 and 4, may require an anesthesia provider's evaluation and order before PACU discharge. An Aldrete of 7 is below the usual threshold of 9.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: When does postanesthesia care begin?
options: After the first PACU vital signs
questions.explanation: Recovery begins in the OR; postanesthesia care starts at extubation, with attention to airway, breathing, circulation, pain, and PONV before transport.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are responsibilities of the anesthesia provider until care is formally relinquished in PACU? (Select 4)
options: Obtaining surgical consent for any return to the OR
questions.explanation: The anesthesia provider remains responsible for airway, hemodynamics, pain, nausea, and an adequate handoff until care is relinquished. The operative note and surgical consent belong to the surgeon.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient arrives in PACU still hypoxemic after extubation. The PACU nurse is admitting another patient. What is the BEST action?
options: Leave the patient on oxygen and return after the next case
Ask a nursing assistant to watch the monitor
Stay, treat, and hand off when stable and a nurse is ready
Give report quickly and leave for the next case
questions.explanation: The anesthesia provider keeps responsibility until a stable patient is handed to a dedicated nurse ready to assume care. Leaving early or delegating to unqualified staff violates that responsibility.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Before giving report, which conditions should be met?
options: PACU orders signed by the surgeon
First PACU vital signs documented by the nurse
Monitors on, stable, and a nurse ready
questions.explanation: Report occurs once appropriate monitors are applied, the patient is stable, and a dedicated PACU nurse is ready to assume responsibility. Full orientation isn't required before report.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which elements belong in a PACU handoff? (Select 5)
options: Fluids and volume status (EBL, urine output, IV fluids)
questions.explanation: Handoff includes ID and allergies, procedure, anesthetic, medications and reversal, antibiotic timing, IV access, fluids and volume status, areas of concern, and the postanesthesia plan. Insurance status isn't part of clinical handoff.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which items in a PACU report help the nurse anticipate problems? (Select 4)
options: Time and dose of the last opioid
questions.explanation: Opioid timing, reversal, antibiotic timing, and the provider's main concerns help the nurse anticipate respiratory depression, residual block, redosing, and complications. The distractors don't affect PACU care.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: During report, which statement BEST reflects the "top three concerns" component for a patient with OSA after a laparoscopic hysterectomy with a JP drain?
options: "Watch for airway obstruction and bleeding from the right JP drain."
"She did fine; nothing to worry about."
"Her case was uncomplicated, so routine PACU care applies to her today."
questions.explanation: A systematic report names the most likely problems so the nurse knows what to watch for, here obstruction from OSA and drain bleeding. The other statements give the nurse nothing specific to act on.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which order of a systematic PACU report is MOST complete?
options: Vital signs, then surgeon's name, then orders and leave
Basics, course, meds, systems, I&Os, lines, concerns
Orders first, then allergies, then procedure
questions.explanation: A systematic report covers age, sex, allergies, ASA, procedure and anesthetic; the course; significant medications with timing; pertinent systems; intake and output; lines and drains; top concerns; orders; and questions.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why is antibiotic dose and time specifically important in the PACU handoff?
options: It guides the choice of reversal agent
It determines the patient's discharge phase
It sets when redosing is due
It predicts the risk of PONV
questions.explanation: Knowing the antibiotic and timing prevents missed or duplicated doses and allows correct redosing. It doesn't guide PONV, reversal, or phase decisions.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient got midazolam 2 mg at 0730, hydromorphone 2 mg at 0941, and ketamine 50 mg at 0800. Which detail in the report MOST helps the PACU nurse?
questions.explanation: Recent opioid timing (here 2 mg hydromorphone near the end) predicts respiratory depression risk in PACU. The other details don't guide monitoring.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which transport preparations are appropriate before leaving the OR? (Select 4)
options: Leave the airway kit behind to lighten the bed
Confirm PACU is ready to receive the patient
Ensure an oxygen source for transport
Disconnect the monitor to save time
questions.explanation: Confirming readiness, appropriate monitoring, medications, equipment, and oxygen are part of safe transport. Removing equipment or monitoring increases risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Unstable patient is going from the OR to the ICU after vascular surgery. What should travel with the patient?
options: Monitors, airway gear, oxygen, and drugs
Nothing extra, since the ICU has everything
A nurse without the anesthesia provider
questions.explanation: Unstable patients need monitoring, airway and oxygen support, and drugs during transport, and an anesthesia team member accompanies them. The receiving unit's equipment doesn't help en route.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which professional behaviors are expected of the anesthesia provider in PACU? (Select 4)
options: Lead by example with infection control
Ask if staff have questions before leaving
Delegate report to the OR nurse
questions.explanation: Professionalism, teamwork, offering help, inviting questions, and infection control are expected. Leaving on arrival or delegating report violates the standards.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: You have another case starting, and your PACU patient remains hypertensive. Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Cancel the next case without communication
Hand off to the PACU anesthesia provider
Give a large antihypertensive bolus and leave
Leave and let the nurse call the surgeon
questions.explanation: Consulting PACU anesthesia staff and handing over a clear plan ensures ongoing management while you return to the OR. Leaving without a plan or a large unmonitored bolus is unsafe.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU nurse admits a patient at 1000. Under the minimum standard of every 5 min for the first 15 min, then every 15 min, how many vital sign recordings are documented by 1100, counting the admission set?
questions.explanation: Recordings at 1000, 1005, 1010, 1015, then 1030, 1045, and 1100 = 7. 6 omits one. 12 assumes every 5 min for an hour. 4 assumes every 15 min from the start.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Same minimum documentation schedule, starting at 1400. When is the first 15-minute-interval recording after the initial frequent checks?
questions.explanation: Frequent checks at 1400, 1405, 1410, and 1415 cover the first 15 min; the next recording is 15 min later at 1430. 1415 is the last 5-min check. 1420 continues 5-min checks. 1445 skips a recording.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which findings must the PACU nurse document at minimum on admission and discharge? (Select 5)
options: Level of consciousness and mental status
questions.explanation: Minimum documentation includes temperature, consciousness, mental status, neuromuscular function, hydration, and nausea. Labs aren't routine minimum documentation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which monitors are applied continuously to every PACU patient at minimum? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Every patient should have continuous pulse oximetry and at least a single-lead ECG, with BP measured frequently. Capnography is for ventilated or at-risk patients. Extra leads are for those at risk of ischemia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which PACU patient MOST needs capnography?
options: Patient still intubated on a ventilator
Child after ear tubes with a mask anesthetic, now awake
Patient after cataract surgery with topical anesthesia
Healthy patient after a hand block alone
questions.explanation: Capnography is needed for mechanically ventilated patients and those at risk for compromised ventilation. The other patients are low risk. Discrepancy flag: a course note says capnography isn't required in PACU; that is true for routine patients but not for ventilated or high-risk ones.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with known CAD had a vascular procedure. Which ECG monitoring is MOST appropriate?
options: Add precordial leads such as V3–V6
A single lead II is sufficient after vascular surgery
No ECG once BP is stable
questions.explanation: Extra leads, particularly precordial V3–V6, are appropriate when left ventricular ischemia is likely. Single-lead monitoring may miss ischemia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient's PACU orders are incomplete: no analgesic or antiemetic orders and no oxygen weaning plan. What is the anesthesia provider's responsibility?
options: Write orders if a problem occurs
Let the PACU nurse decide treatment
Leave the orders for the surgeon
questions.explanation: An accurate and complete order set is part of the anesthesia provider's PACU responsibilities. Leaving gaps forces delays when problems occur.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes why the transition from OR to PACU is a dangerous time?
options: Drugs stop redistributing once the volatile is turned off
PACU staff have more training than OR staff
Patients are fully recovered by transport
Monitoring and expertise drop while drug effects persist
questions.explanation: Patients leave a highly controlled environment, often travel minimally monitored, and are handed to a team with a different skill set while anesthetics are still redistributing. That combination makes the transition risky.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which situations require the anesthesia provider to stay with the patient before handing off? (Select 2)
options: The nurse is ready and the patient is stable
The surgeon has left the room
No dedicated PACU nurse is available
The patient is awake and stable on monitors
questions.explanation: Handoff requires a stable patient and a dedicated nurse ready to assume care.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU nurse asks about an IV that infiltrated during the case. Which handoff element covers this?
questions.explanation: IV access, including sites, problems, and removals, is part of handoff.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which handoff element MOST helps the nurse anticipate residual weakness?
questions.explanation: Knowing whether and when reversal was given helps the nurse watch for residual blockade.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which handoff element MOST helps the nurse plan fluid management?
options: EBL, urine output, and IV fluids given
Antibiotic name, dose, and time given
questions.explanation: Fluid and volume status (EBL, UOP, IVF) guides fluid management.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which handoff items should be stated for a patient with a JP drain and arterial line removed in the OR? (Select 2)
options: Lines placed or removed, including the arterial line
questions.explanation: Lines and drains, including removed lines, belong in handoff.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which component of a systematic report includes "33-year-old woman, PCN allergy, ASA 3, lap-assisted hysterectomy under GETA with TAP blocks"?
questions.explanation: Age, sex, allergies, ASA, surgery, and anesthetic type come first in a systematic report.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the PACU as related to the OR?
options: A place where anesthesia responsibility ends
A lower-acuity area needing little attention
questions.explanation: The PACU is an extension of the OR, and vigilance must be maintained.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which handoff habit MOST improves safety?
questions.explanation: Standardized handoffs or checklists, often facility-specific, improve completeness.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: After handoff, what should you do before leaving the bedside?
options: Ask the nurse for questions or needs
Tell the nurse to call the surgeon for problems
questions.explanation: Asking for questions confirms understanding before you leave.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: After your patient leaves PACU, what is good practice?
options: Assume no news means no problems
Review the case if a complaint is filed
questions.explanation: Following up on how your patient did in PACU closes the loop and helps you learn.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which factors determine the level of postanesthesia care a patient needs? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Comorbidities, procedure type and duration, and anesthetic type determine triage. Insurance, location, and day don't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are goals of postanesthesia triage? (Select 4)
options: Longer PACU stays for every patient
Right level of care for each patient
Lower costs and conserved staff resources
questions.explanation: Triage matches care to need, reduces complications and costs, conserves staff, and improves satisfaction.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient after open AAA repair with ongoing volume shifts needs close monitoring. Which recovery level fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Major surgery with volume shifts needs Phase I or ICU-level intensity. Phase II is for less intensive, discharge-focused care. Phase III is for patients who met Phase I criteria but await a bed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients typically need Phase I recovery? (Select 4)
options: Patient after cataract surgery with oral diazepam and topical
Patient awake after a propofol colonoscopy
Patient with significant volume shifts or transfusion
questions.explanation: General anesthesia, major surgery, volume shifts or transfusion, significant pain, and regional catheters call for Phase I. Topical eye cases and awake propofol-only colonoscopies are typical Phase II or fast-track patients.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which Phase I staffing description in current practice is MOST accurate?
options: 1:6 once the first vital signs are recorded
1:1 for every patient regardless of stability
questions.explanation: Phase I requires intense care and constant vigilance. ASPAN staffing recommends a 1:2 nurse-to-patient ratio, with 1:1 for unconscious, unstable, or airway-supported patients. Discrepancy flag: the course describes Phase I as one-on-one care; that applies to the highest-acuity patients rather than every Phase I patient.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are Phase I priorities? (Select 4)
options: Discontinuing or adapting IV fluids per enhanced recovery
Stable airway with adequate ventilation and oxygenation
questions.explanation: Phase I focuses on airway, ventilation, oxygenation, hemodynamics, analgesia, PONV, oral intake, and IV management. Discharge education and transport are Phase II priorities.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are criteria for discharge from Phase I? (Select 4)
options: Ability to move extremities on command
Adequate oxygen saturation on room air
questions.explanation: Phase I discharge requires airway and ventilation adequacy, hemodynamic stability, purposeful movement, full alertness, and adequate saturation on room air. Ambulation and discharge teaching belong to Phase II.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are criteria for discharge from Phase II? (Select 5)
options: Arterial line removed within the last hour
questions.explanation: Phase II discharge considers pain, hemodynamics, nausea, fluid intake, ambulation, understanding instructions, and safe transport home. Arterial lines aren't typical Phase II issues.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 65-year-old has cataract surgery with oral diazepam and topical anesthesia. Which recovery level fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Patients leaving the OR awake after light sedation and local or topical anesthesia fit Phase II, which focuses on preparing for discharge. Phase I and ICU are for higher-acuity patients.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 45-year-old had a propofol-only colonoscopy and is awake and talking in the procedure room. Which recovery level fits BEST?
questions.explanation: Propofol-only colonoscopy patients who leave awake typically go to Phase II.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which BEST defines fast-tracking?
options: Moving a patient from the OR directly to the ICU
Moving a patient from Phase I directly home
questions.explanation: Fast-tracking means bypassing Phase I and admitting the patient from the OR directly to Phase II. Report is still required.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients are reasonable candidates for fast-tracking? (Select 3)
options: Patient after a spinal for knee arthroscopy
Patient after MAC for a superficial procedure
Patient with a new epidural catheter
Patient after a peripheral nerve block for hand surgery
Patient after light sedation with local infiltration
Patient after general endotracheal anesthesia for laparoscopy
questions.explanation: MAC, light sedation, superficial and peripheral procedures, and local or peripheral regional techniques qualify. Neuraxial techniques (spinal or epidural) don't, and GA patients generally need Phase I.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why is a patient who had a spinal for knee arthroscopy NOT a fast-track candidate?
options: Spinal patients need ICU-level care after any neuraxial block
questions.explanation: Fast-track examples include MAC, light sedation, and peripheral regional, but not neuraxial anesthesia, which brings sympathectomy, motor block, and voiding issues. The other options are wrong.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which benefits are attributed to fast-tracking? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Fast-tracking can be cost-effective and improve satisfaction. Discharge assessment and policies still apply.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which requirement must be in place for a facility to fast-track patients?
options: Approval from each patient's insurer in advance
questions.explanation: Fast-tracking requires established policies and procedures regarding selection criteria with input from the anesthesia department. Criteria may include scoring systems, status, vital signs, procedure, and complications. Discrepancy flag: criteria are often site specific and may use different scales, such as a modified Aldrete.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient meets Phase I discharge criteria at 1900, but no inpatient bed is available. Which care level applies?
questions.explanation: Phase III covers patients who met criteria to leave Phase I but can't go elsewhere, such as when no inpatient bed is available. They are managed as inpatients in the same physical location.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements about Phase III extended care are accurate? (Select 3)
options: It serves patients awaiting an inpatient location
It occurs in the same location as Phase I and II
It is a form of fast-tracking
It is the first recovery stage after GA
questions.explanation: Phase III is extended care in the PACU location for patients who met Phase I criteria but have nowhere to go, managed as inpatients. It isn't the first stage, doesn't need one-to-one care, and isn't fast-tracking.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which recovery option fits a patient who needs 23-hr observation after outpatient surgery?
options: Phase II discharge home the same evening
questions.explanation: Short stay or 23-hr admission serves patients who need observation but not inpatient admission. Fast-track and Phase II discharge send patients home. ICU is for critical care.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which Phase I complication would make a patient unsuitable to move to Phase II?
questions.explanation: Airway compromise, cardiovascular depression, uncontrolled pain, nausea, and delirium are Phase I complications that must resolve before moving on. Thirst and discharge needs are Phase II matters.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Where do patients recovering from MRI under anesthesia, CT, IR, or cardiac cath procedures typically recover?
options: No recovery is needed after NORA procedures
A NORA recovery area matched to acuity
questions.explanation: Recovery levels include NORA recovery for patients after CT, MRI, IR, cath lab, pediatric, and radiation procedures, matched to their acuity. They still need postanesthesia care.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which Phase II priority distinguishes it MOST from Phase I?
options: Management of regional catheters and invasive lines
questions.explanation: Phase II focuses on mobility, oral intake, analgesia, discharge teaching, and prescriptions. Airway, hemodynamics, and catheter management are Phase I priorities.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are recognized possible Phase I complications? (Select 4)
options: Inability to arrange a ride home
questions.explanation: Phase I complications include airway compromise, cardiovascular depression, pain, nausea or vomiting, delirium, and procedure-specific issues. Transport and prescriptions are Phase II concerns.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient in Phase II after hand surgery has a pain score of 3, stable vitals, is drinking, walks with a steady gait, and understands instructions, but her ride won't arrive for 3 hr. What is MOST appropriate?
options: Wait for safe transportation before discharge
Discharge her by taxi alone with written instructions
questions.explanation: Safe transportation is a Phase II discharge requirement. Returning to Phase I or ICU isn't needed for a stable patient.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which locations or levels are part of postanesthesia triage? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Triage options include ICU, Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, short stay, and NORA recovery.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient after MAC for a breast biopsy is awake and stable leaving the OR. Which pathway is BEST?
questions.explanation: MAC with a superficial procedure and an awake, stable patient fits fast-tracking.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the modified Aldrete scale that scores circulation by mmHg from preop BP: patient takes deep breaths and coughs, SpO2 94% on room air, fully awake, BP within 15 mmHg of preop, moves all four extremities. Score?
questions.explanation: Respiration 2, SpO2 >92% on room air 2, fully awake 2, BP within ±20 mmHg 2, moves four extremities 2 = 10. Each lower total drops a point that the findings earn.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Same mmHg-based modified Aldrete: deep breaths and cough, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula (91% on room air), arousable on calling, BP within 10 mmHg of preop, moves all four extremities. Score?
questions.explanation: Respiration 2, needs O2 to maintain above 90% = 1, arousable on calling = 1, circulation 2, activity 2 = 8. A score of 9 counts either O2 or consciousness as 2. 10 counts both as 2. 7 drops an extra point.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Same mmHg-based modified Aldrete: shallow breathing, SpO2 93% on room air, fully awake, BP 30 mmHg below preop, moves only two extremities after a spinal. Score?
questions.explanation: Dyspnea or shallow breathing 1, SpO2 >92% on room air 2, fully awake 2, BP within 20–50 mmHg 1, moves two extremities 1 = 7. Each wrong answer miscounts one category.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the mmHg-based modified Aldrete scale, what total score is generally required for discharge from Phase I?
options: At least 8 with no zero in any category
questions.explanation: A score of 9 or more is the usual discharge threshold. Some policies add that no category may score zero, but the core threshold is 9.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the version of the modified Aldrete that scores hemodynamics by percent of baseline MAP: baseline MAP 90, current MAP 70. What is the hemodynamic score?
options: Can't be scored without heart rate
questions.explanation: (90 − 70) ÷ 90 ≈ 22% below baseline, which falls in the 15–30% band for a score of 1. Within 15% scores 2; more than 30% below scores 0. Heart rate isn't part of this category.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Same MAP-based Aldrete: baseline MAP 100, current MAP 88. Hemodynamic score?
questions.explanation: 12 ÷ 100 = 12% below baseline, within 15%, which scores 2. An absolute MAP cutoff isn't part of this scale.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Same MAP-based Aldrete: baseline MAP 95, current MAP 60. Hemodynamic score?
questions.explanation: (95 − 60) ÷ 95 ≈ 37% below baseline, more than 30%, which scores 0. Symptoms don't change the numeric score.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Two versions of the modified Aldrete score differ on oxygen saturation. Which pairing is accurate?
options: One awards 2 for SpO2 above 92% on room air; another uses above 90%
Both award 2 for SpO2 above 95% on room air
One awards 2 points for SpO2 above 90% on supplemental O2 by mask
questions.explanation: One commonly used modified Aldrete awards 2 for SpO2 above 92% on room air; another version awards 2 for maintaining above 90% on room air. Both score supplemental O2 needs lower. Discrepancy flag: course tables show both versions, so confirm which one your facility uses.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Two versions of the modified Aldrete score differ on circulation. Which pairing is accurate?
options: Both use heart rate within 20% of preop
±20 mmHg from preop versus % change in MAP
One uses MAP above 65; the other uses SBP above 90
questions.explanation: One version scores BP within ±20 mmHg of preop as 2 (20–50 mmHg = 1, over 50 = 0); another scores MAP within 15% of baseline as 2 (15–30% = 1, over 30% below = 0). Neither uses HR or absolute cutoffs.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the MAP-based Aldrete version: awake and oriented, moves all extremities, MAP 10% below baseline, tachypneic with a good cough, SpO2 93% on 2 L. Total?
questions.explanation: Consciousness 2, activity 2, hemodynamics 2, tachypnea with good cough 1, requires supplemental oxygen 1 = 8. The distractors miscount the respiratory or oxygen categories.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the MAP-based version: arousable with minimal stimulation, some weakness in movement, MAP 20% below baseline, breathes deeply, SpO2 92% on room air. Total?
questions.explanation: Consciousness 1, activity 1, hemodynamics 1, respiratory 2, SpO2 above 90% on room air 2 = 7. The distractors add or drop a point.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the postanesthesia discharge scoring system (PADSS): vital signs within 15% of preop, steady gait, minimal nausea treated with oral medication, pain controlled with oral analgesics and acceptable, no dressing changes. Score?
questions.explanation: Vital signs 2, activity 2, nausea 2, pain 2, bleeding 2 = 10. Each lower total drops a point the findings earn.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PADSS: vital signs 30% from preop, needs assistance to walk, nausea treated with IV medication, pain controlled and acceptable, minimal bleeding. Score?
questions.explanation: Vital signs 20–40% = 1, requires assistance = 1, parenteral treatment = 1, pain yes = 2, minimal bleeding = 2, total 7. The distractors miscount one category.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PADSS: vital signs within 10% of preop, steady gait, minimal nausea, pain not controlled with oral analgesics, two dressing changes for oozing. Score?
questions.explanation: Vital signs 2, activity 2, nausea 2, pain not controlled 1, up to two dressing changes 1 = 7. This patient isn't ready for home discharge (threshold 9).

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which categories are scored in the postanesthesia discharge scoring system? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: PADSS scores vital signs, activity, nausea and vomiting, pain, and surgical bleeding. Oxygen saturation is a modified Aldrete category.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which categories are scored in the mmHg-based modified Aldrete system? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: The modified Aldrete scores respiration, oxygenation, consciousness, circulation, and activity. Pain is scored in PADSS.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which general findings indicate readiness for PACU discharge? (Select 4)
options: Requires jaw thrust to maintain patency
questions.explanation: Patients should be arousable, oriented, managing their airway, hemodynamically stable, able to communicate, without apparent surgical complications, and with controlled pain.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient scores 9 on the modified Aldrete but has a rapidly expanding neck hematoma after thyroidectomy. What is MOST appropriate?
options: Discharge after one more set of vitals
questions.explanation: Discharge also requires no apparent surgical complications. Scores support judgment but don't override clinical findings like an expanding hematoma.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient scores 9 on PADSS after an outpatient procedure but has no escort and lives alone. What is the BEST action?
options: Arrange a responsible adult before discharge
Discharge with instructions to call if needed
Discharge by taxi alone since the score is 9
questions.explanation: Safe transport and an escort are required for ambulatory discharge, independent of the score. ICU admission isn't needed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using PADSS: vital signs 45% from preop, steady gait, minimal nausea, pain controlled, minimal bleeding. Score and readiness?
questions.explanation: Vital signs over 40% = 0, activity 2, nausea 2, pain 2, bleeding 2 = 8, below 9. The vital sign change needs evaluation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the mmHg-based modified Aldrete: apneic needing ventilation, SpO2 88% on O2, not responding, BP 55 mmHg below preop, no movement. Score?
questions.explanation: Each category scores 0 for apnea, saturation under 90% with O2, unresponsiveness, BP over 50 mmHg from preop, and no movement.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Using the mmHg-based modified Aldrete: deep breaths, SpO2 93% on room air, arousable on calling, BP within 20 mmHg, moves all four. Score and readiness?
questions.explanation: Respiration 2, SpO2 2, consciousness 1, circulation 2, activity 2 = 9, meeting the usual threshold.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which PADSS findings each earn the maximum points in their category? (Select 3)
options: Minimal nausea treated with oral medication
questions.explanation: Steady gait, minimal or oral-treated nausea, and minimal bleeding earn 2. The others earn 1.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which finding prevents Phase I discharge despite good scores elsewhere?
questions.explanation: Inadequate oxygen saturation on room air is a Phase I discharge consideration.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient meets home discharge criteria?
options: Stable vitals, can't walk, no escort
questions.explanation: Phase II discharge requires stable vitals, ambulation, fluid intake, controlled pain and nausea, minimal bleeding, understanding of instructions, and safe transport.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PADSS: vital signs within 15%, needs assistance to walk, minimal nausea, pain acceptable on oral analgesics, minimal bleeding. Score?
questions.explanation: Vital signs 2, activity 1, nausea 2, pain 2, bleeding 2 = 9.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Most common physiologic cause of upper airway obstruction in PACU?
questions.explanation: Loss of pharyngeal muscle tone with posterior tongue displacement is the leading cause. Laryngospasm and hematoma are important but less common. Bronchospasm is lower airway.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient snores loudly in PACU with intercostal retractions and SpO2 89%. What is the FIRST step?
options: Succinylcholine 0.5 mg/kg IV, then mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Snoring with retractions suggests soft-tissue obstruction, which simple maneuvers (positioning, jaw thrust, suction, stimulation) often relieve. Drugs and reintubation follow if needed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which simple maneuvers often relieve PACU airway obstruction? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Positioning, jaw thrust, suctioning, and stimulating the patient often open an obstructed airway. Relaxants and deeper anesthesia worsen obstruction unless intubating.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with obstruction after jaw thrust still has partial obstruction; she is groggy but responds to voice. What is the BEST next step?
options: Place an oral airway in the responsive patient
Remove stimulation to let her rest
questions.explanation: A nasal airway is better tolerated in a semi-responsive patient than an oral airway, which can trigger gagging, vomiting, or laryngospasm. Sedation and less stimulation worsen obstruction.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which drug class MOST commonly causes hypoventilation in PACU?
questions.explanation: Residual volatile agents, propofol, and opioids are the most common causes of hypoventilation. Residual block contributes but is less common.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which mechanisms contribute to compromised ventilation and oxygenation after general anesthesia? (Select 4)
options: Blunted ventilatory response to hypercarbia and hypoxemia
questions.explanation: Anesthetics blunt chemoreceptor responses, opioids and sedatives depress medullary drive, atelectasis causes shunt and V/Q mismatch, and GA reduces FRC. The distractors describe opposite effects.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient's preop FRC is 2.5 L. Using a 20% reduction after GA, what is the expected FRC?
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 0.8 = 2.0 L. 2.25 is a 10% reduction. 0.5 is the reduction itself. 3.0 adds 20%.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Obese patient's preop FRC is 1.6 L. With a 15% reduction after GA, what is the expected FRC?
questions.explanation: 1.6 × 0.85 = 1.36 L. 1.84 adds 15%. 0.24 is the reduction. 1.45 uses about 9%.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients are MOST affected by reduced FRC after anesthesia? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Reduced FRC impacts patients with lung illness, obesity, OSA, older adults, and children most. Healthy young adults tolerate it better.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why can a healthy patient on 4 L nasal cannula have SpO2 98% while hypoventilating?
questions.explanation: Healthy adults can maintain oxygenation, which can mask poor ventilation. Capnography or ABG reveals rising CO2.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after sevoflurane is hypoventilating and becoming more sedated. Which mechanism links these?
questions.explanation: Volatiles are eliminated through the lungs; hypoventilation slows washout and can keep patients sedated, and rising CO2 adds sedation. Hypoventilation doesn't increase metabolism or speed elimination.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which causes of compromised ventilation and oxygenation should be considered in PACU? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Soft-tissue relaxation, residual weakness, external compression from hematoma, and laryngospasm are listed causes. The distractors don't cause compromised ventilation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient after anterior cervical fusion in PACU has new stridor, neck swelling, and difficulty swallowing. What is the MOST likely cause and step?
options: Hematoma; call the surgeon and prepare the airway
questions.explanation: Neck swelling with stridor after neck surgery suggests hematoma; notify the surgeon, prepare for emergent airway management, and open the wound if needed. The other diagnoses don't fit neck swelling.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which steps manage compromised ventilation in PACU? (Select 5)
options: Optimize position and use airway adjuncts
Give more opioid to settle the patient
Reverse benzodiazepines, opioids, or relaxants as appropriate
questions.explanation: Positioning, adjuncts, stimulation, reversal, emergency airway preparation, and surgeon notification are listed. More opioid worsens hypoventilation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Before transport, which finding confirms readiness to leave the OR from an airway standpoint?
options: Coughing on the tube at deep levels
Managing own airway and past stage II
SpO2 above 90% on 100% O2 with jaw thrust
questions.explanation: Patients should manage their own airway and be past stage II into stage I before leaving the OR. Needing jaw thrust or coughing at stage II indicates they aren't ready.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 5-year-old in PACU has partial obstruction while supine. Which position BEST supports the airway during transport and recovery?
options: Sitting upright with neck flexed and chin down
questions.explanation: Pediatric patients are transported lateral and head-down with blow-by oxygen, which lets the tongue fall forward and secretions drain. Flexion worsens obstruction.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Toddler needs mask ventilation in PACU. A pad under the head flexes the neck. Why?
options: Children's necks naturally extend when supine
A pillow under the head aligns the airway in children
Children have small occiputs that tilt the head back
Large occiput bends the neck; use a shoulder roll
questions.explanation: Children's large occiput flexes the neck when supine, so a shoulder roll rather than a head pillow may improve alignment. The other statements reverse the anatomy.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which factors contribute to airway edema at the end of surgery? (Select 4)
options: Short supine case with minimal fluid
questions.explanation: Long prone or steep Trendelenburg cases, large crystalloid volumes, airway or neck procedures, and anaphylaxis can cause airway edema. Short supine cases and spinals don't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: After 6 hr of steep Trendelenburg prostatectomy with 5 L crystalloid, the patient's face and sclera are edematous. What is the BEST next step before extubation?
options: Assess airway edema with a cuff leak test
Extubate and place a nasal airway
Give a diuretic and extubate in 5 min if SpO2 is normal
questions.explanation: Facial and scleral edema suggests airway edema, so its extent should be assessed before extubation; delayed extubation may be safer. Deep extubation and quick extubation add risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which finding suggests that significant airway edema may make extubation unsafe?
options: No cuff leak with the cuff down
Normal tidal volumes on pressure support
questions.explanation: An absent cuff leak suggests airway swelling. Tidal volumes, command following, and oxygenation don't assess upper airway caliber.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient after extubation has upper airway obstruction that relieves with jaw thrust but returns when released. What is the MOST likely reason in a patient given 0.8 mg hydromorphone and 2 mg midazolam?
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury from intubation
questions.explanation: Relief with jaw thrust indicates soft-tissue obstruction, made worse by sedatives and opioids. Nerve injury, bronchospasm, and pneumothorax wouldn't respond to jaw thrust.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient in PACU after tonsillectomy becomes hypoxic with pink frothy sputum after an episode of obstruction. What explains this?
options: Fluid overload from intraoperative IV fluids
questions.explanation: Airway obstruction can lead to negative-pressure pulmonary edema when the patient inspires forcefully against a closed airway. The other diagnoses don't fit the timing.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient needs reversal of benzodiazepines and opioids readied MOST before PACU arrival?
options: Older patient with OSA given midazolam and hydromorphone
Young patient after a peripheral block alone with no sedation
Patient after spinal with no sedation
Patient after a short propofol MAC
questions.explanation: Combined benzodiazepines and opioids in an older patient with OSA create high risk for respiratory depression and obstruction. The other patients received little or no sedative.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which adjunct is BEST tolerated in a semi-conscious patient with obstruction?
questions.explanation: NPAs are tolerated in semi-conscious patients. OPAs stimulate gag and laryngospasm.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with obstruction in PACU responds to jaw thrust but not when released. Which option keeps the airway open while she recovers?
options: Remove the adjuncts and observe closely
questions.explanation: Leaving an OPA or NPA in place as needed maintains patency.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which steps optimize ventilation and perfusion before leaving the OR? (Select 2)
options: Supine flat positioning of obese patients
questions.explanation: Recruitment and adequate BP optimize ventilation and perfusion.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which finding indicates hypoventilation even though SpO2 is 97% on 3 L?
questions.explanation: Supplemental O2 masks hypoventilation; elevated EtCO2 reveals it.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which nerve mediates the reflex responsible for laryngospasm?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is an exaggerated glottic closure reflex mediated by the superior laryngeal nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles but isn't the reflex afferent here.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Child after extubation makes a high-pitched crowing sound with each breath and SpO2 is 92%. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Stridor indicates some air movement, suggesting partial laryngospasm. Complete laryngospasm is silent with paradoxical chest movement. Bronchospasm causes expiratory wheezing.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Child after extubation has no airflow sounds, paradoxical chest and abdominal movement, and falling SpO2. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Silence with paradoxical chest movement means complete glottic closure. Partial laryngospasm produces stridor. Central apnea has no respiratory effort.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which factors precipitate laryngospasm? (Select 5)
options: Secretions or blood in the airway
Deep anesthesia with a still patient
questions.explanation: Secretions, blood, stage II extubation, redistribution to a light plane, unanticipated stimulus, pediatric age, and URI precipitate laryngospasm. Deep anesthesia with no stimulation lowers risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: After deep extubation, a child is transported to PACU while still in stage II. Which complication is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Stage II carries heightened airway reflexes; patients extubated deep should progress through stage II to stage I before going to PACU. MH, bronchospasm, and hypoglycemia aren't linked to stage II specifically.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Child develops laryngospasm in PACU with SpO2 90%. What is the FIRST set of actions?
options: Succinylcholine 1 mg/kg IV and immediate intubation
questions.explanation: Initial steps are oxygen, suction to clear secretions, jaw thrust with pressure at the laryngospasm notch, and positive pressure. Drugs, intubation, and surgical airways escalate if those fail.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Where is pressure applied for Larson's maneuver?
options: Behind the earlobe, near the condyle
At the angle of the mandible, pushing downward
questions.explanation: Larson's maneuver applies firm bilateral pressure cephalad and medially in the notch between the mastoid process and the posterior mandibular ramus near the condyle. Cricoid pressure doesn't relieve laryngospasm.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Laryngospasm persists despite O2, suction, jaw thrust, Larson's maneuver, and CPAP; SpO2 is 80%. Which drug is BEST next if no IV relaxant is ready but propofol is in hand?
options: Ondansetron 4 mg IV for associated retching
questions.explanation: A subinduction propofol dose deepens anesthesia and can break laryngospasm. Succinylcholine is definitive if it fails. Midazolam is slow, and the others don't treat laryngospasm.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 20 kg child has laryngospasm unresponsive to CPAP and propofol. Using succinylcholine 0.5 mg/kg IV, what dose?
questions.explanation: 0.5 × 20 = 10 mg. 1 mg is a decimal slip. 100 mg is 5 mg/kg. 20 mg is 1 mg/kg.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 70 kg adult with persistent laryngospasm. What is the dose range for IV succinylcholine at 0.25–1 mg/kg?
questions.explanation: 0.25 × 70 = 17.5 mg; 1 × 70 = 70 mg. Many references cite 0.1–0.5 mg/kg as effective; lower doses can break spasm without full paralysis. Discrepancy flag: the course range (0.25–1 mg/kg) is higher at the top than many airway references. The other options are decimal or doubling errors.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 12 kg child has laryngospasm and no IV. Using IM succinylcholine 4 mg/kg, what dose?
questions.explanation: 4 × 12 = 48 mg IM, often with atropine. 4.8 is a decimal slip. 12 mg uses 1 mg/kg. 24 mg uses 2 mg/kg.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which interventions are part of laryngospasm treatment? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Oxygen, suction, jaw thrust, Larson's maneuver, CPAP, subinduction propofol, and succinylcholine are standard. Removing oxygen worsens hypoxemia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: What is the definitive treatment of laryngospasm that fails positive pressure and maneuvers?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine relaxes the vocal cords and is the gold standard when other measures fail. More CPAP has already failed. Lidocaine and dexamethasone don't reliably break established spasm.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which strategy BEST prevents laryngospasm at extubation in a child with secretions?
options: Extubate in stage II to avoid coughing
Extubate during light anesthesia while the child moves
Extubate without suctioning to avoid stimulation
Suction, then extubate awake or deep
questions.explanation: Clearing secretions and extubating either fully awake or deep (avoiding stage II) lowers risk. Stage II extubation and leaving secretions raise risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why is laryngospasm more common in children with a recent URI?
options: URIs lower the risk of airway events by drying secretions
questions.explanation: Airway hyperreactivity persists after viral infections, increasing laryngospasm and bronchospasm. The other options reverse the effect.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Laryngospasm persists despite succinylcholine and SpO2 continues to fall with failed intubation. What is the BEST next step?
options: Wait for spontaneous resolution with CPAP
questions.explanation: If intubation fails and oxygenation fails, a surgical airway or jet ventilation is the final rescue step. Waiting or more drug delays rescue.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Partial laryngospasm with stridor is present. Which combination is MOST appropriate first?
questions.explanation: Partial laryngospasm often responds to PPV with O2 and Larson's maneuver.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which signs distinguish complete from partial laryngospasm? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Complete laryngospasm is silent with paradoxical movement. Stridor indicates partial.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which school of thought exists for laryngospasm unresponsive to succinylcholine and PPV?
options: Wait for spontaneous resolution with CPAP
questions.explanation: Attempted intubation is one approach, followed by cric or jet ventilation if needed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which statements about Larson's maneuver are accurate? (Select 2)
options: Pressure is applied over the cricoid cartilage
It requires a neuromuscular blocker first
Pressure is applied bilaterally in the notch behind the earlobe
It's combined with jaw thrust and positive pressure
questions.explanation: Larson's maneuver applies firm bilateral pressure cephalad and medially in the laryngospasm notch, combined with jaw thrust and CPAP.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient 20 min after laparotomy: BP 188/102, HR 112, restless, SpO2 88% on 2 L, RR 26. What is the FIRST step?
options: Give hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV for pain
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia and hypercapnia cause hypertension and tachycardia and must be ruled out first; labetalol or opioids could worsen an unrecognized respiratory problem. Pain and bladder distension are checked after airway and breathing.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are common causes of hypertension in PACU? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Emergence sympathetic stimulation, pain, the endotracheal tube, bladder distension, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, preexisting hypertension, and fluid overload contribute. Neuraxial sympathectomy lowers BP.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after urologic surgery has BP 178/96, HR 104, and suprapubic fullness; pain is 2/10 and SpO2 98%. Which step is MOST appropriate?
options: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV for presumed incisional pain
Bladder scan and drain if distended
questions.explanation: Bladder distension is a common, easily treated cause of hypertension. Treating the BP or giving opioids misses the cause.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with long-standing hypertension who skipped her morning antihypertensives has BP 182/98, no pain, normal SpO2 and EtCO2, empty bladder. What is the BEST step?
options: Reintubate to control the stress response
questions.explanation: After ruling out hypoxia, hypercapnia, pain, and bladder causes, treating with appropriate antihypertensives and resuming home therapy is reasonable. Observation for hours risks complications. Fluids and reintubation aren't indicated.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which finding would point toward fluid overload as the cause of PACU hypertension?
options: Pain score of 8 with tachycardia, guarding, and grimacing
Crackles, rising SpO2 requirement, and a large positive balance
questions.explanation: Hypertension with crackles, worsening oxygenation, and a large positive fluid balance suggests overload. Pain and bladder distension cause hypertension through sympathetic stimulation.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Patient with CAD has BP 190/100 and HR 120 in PACU after excluding hypoxemia. Why is prompt treatment important?
questions.explanation: Hypertension and tachycardia increase myocardial oxygen demand and ischemia risk, and can also increase bleeding. They don't cause hypothermia or ventilatory depression.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which complications can result from untreated PACU hypertension? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension raises myocardial O2 demand, promotes surgical bleeding, and risks cerebrovascular events. The distractors aren't consequences.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Most common cause of hypotension in PACU?
questions.explanation: Hypovolemia, from blood loss, inadequate replacement, or vasodilation, is the most common cause. The other causes are important but less common.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after spinal for knee surgery: BP 82/48, HR 64, warm legs, block to T8. What is the MOST likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Neuraxial anesthesia causes venous pooling and reduces effective circulating volume (relative hypovolemia). The other diagnoses would bring other findings.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 70 kg patient is hypotensive in PACU from hypovolemia. A fluid challenge of 250–500 mL crystalloid is planned. Which bolus is in range and about 5 mL/kg?
questions.explanation: 5 × 70 = 350 mL, within the 250–500 mL range. 35 mL is a decimal slip. 700 mL is 10 mL/kg. 1,400 mL is 20 mL/kg.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient becomes hypotensive (BP 68/40) with HR 128 and hives 5 min after IV cefazolin redose. What is the BEST first drug?
questions.explanation: Hypotension with urticaria after a drug suggests anaphylaxis, and epinephrine is first-line. Phenylephrine treats vasodilation but not mast cell mediators. Antihistamines and fluids are adjuncts.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with known cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) is hypotensive with crackles and JVD after a fluid bolus. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Ventricular dysfunction is a consideration in patients with cardiac disease, and worsening with fluids points to it. Hypovolemia would improve with fluids. The others don't fit.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which steps are appropriate for PACU hypotension? (Select 4)
options: Increase opioids to reduce pain-related vasodilation
Notify the surgeon or cardiology if cardiac function is in question
Lower the head of bed to sitting
questions.explanation: Fluids, a vasopressor, anaphylaxis treatment when suspected, and notification are listed. More opioids worsen hypotension, and sitting reduces preload.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after lap chole: BP 78/44, HR 118, pale, abdominal distension, and drain output rising. What is the BEST response?
options: Treat as bleeding and notify the surgeon
questions.explanation: Hypotension with tachycardia, distension, and rising drain output suggests surgical bleeding. Vasopressors alone mask the problem.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient on dexmedetomidine during the case has HR 46, BP 110/70, alert, no symptoms. What is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: HR below 60 may not need action if the patient is stable and asymptomatic; evaluate the cause (here dex). Drug therapy or pacing is for symptomatic or unstable bradycardia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are causes of postoperative bradycardia? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Dex, beta blockers, MI, opioids, and anticholinesterases (or high spinal) slow HR. Hypovolemia and fever cause tachycardia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient has HR 42, BP 78/44, and dizziness. Which drugs are reasonable first choices?
questions.explanation: Symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension can be treated with an anticholinergic or ephedrine. Beta blockers and phenylephrine slow HR. Adenosine is for SVT.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient has HR 32, BP 60/30, and is unresponsive to atropine. When is electrical therapy appropriate?
questions.explanation: Unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine warrants transcutaneous pacing (or epinephrine or dopamine). Cardioversion and defibrillation treat tachyarrhythmias or arrest.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Most common time for tachycardia after anesthesia?
options: During preoperative holding before any sedation
Emergence and the first 30 min of PACU
questions.explanation: Tachycardia is common on emergence and in the first 30 min of PACU. It often reflects pain, emergence, or hypoxemia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Healthy 25-year-old in PACU has HR 108 after knee arthroscopy; BP 128/76, SpO2 99%, pain 6/10. What is the BEST response?
options: Give a fluid bolus of 2 L
questions.explanation: Tachycardia may not be a concern in a healthy, hemodynamically stable patient, and pain is the likely cause. Rate control and a workup aren't needed. A 2 L bolus is excessive.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: 72-year-old with CAD has HR 118 in PACU after hip surgery; SpO2 97%, Hb 11, pain controlled. Which approach is BEST?
options: Give a large fluid bolus without assessment
Observe; tachycardia is expected after surgery
questions.explanation: In patients with cardiovascular disease, strict rate control reduces myocardial O2 demand. Pain is controlled, so other causes and rate control are addressed.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with tachycardia also has SpO2 86% and agitation. What should be addressed FIRST?
questions.explanation: Tachycardia can be a sign of hypoxemia; airway and ventilation must be ruled out first. Esmolol, opioids, and benzodiazepines can worsen hypoxemia or mask it.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which are perioperative causes of tachycardia? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Pain, anxiety, fever, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, hypovolemia, hypoglycemia, drugs, allergy, beta agonists, thromboembolism, pheochromocytoma, metabolic disorders, tension pneumothorax, anemia, thyroid storm, and withdrawal are listed. Beta blocker overdose causes bradycardia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which serious causes of PACU tachycardia must be considered? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Thyroid storm, thromboembolism, MH, and withdrawal all cause tachycardia and need specific treatment. Hypothermia without shivering and dex tend to slow HR.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with CAD has HR 128 and pain controlled. Which drug is MOST appropriate for short-term rate control?
questions.explanation: Short-acting drugs such as esmolol are often used in PACU because they act quickly and wear off. A large metoprolol bolus risks hypotension. Diltiazem and digoxin are less suited.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why should you bring rate-control drugs with you to PACU for a high-risk cardiac patient?
options: Drugs given in the OR are cheaper than PACU stock
Tachycardia may need immediate treatment in transit
questions.explanation: Taking drugs you may need ensures immediate treatment during transport or early PACU. PACU stocks drugs, but delays can occur.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with a history of pheochromocytoma resection 2 days ago has HR 140 and BP 210/120. What is MOST likely?
options: Opioid withdrawal after surgery from missed doses
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a cause of tachycardia, and recurrence or residual tumor is a concern. The other causes don't typically produce severe hypertension with tachycardia.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which findings in PACU suggest malignant hyperthermia? (Select 4)
options: Normal temperature trends with falling EtCO2
questions.explanation: MH can present in PACU with tachycardia, acidemia, hypoxemia, hypercarbia, rigidity, and hyperthermia; sedation may occur. Bradycardia and falling EtCO2 point elsewhere.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after sevoflurane has HR 130, EtCO2 58 on a capnography line, temp 38.6 °C, and masseter rigidity. What is the BEST next step?
questions.explanation: MH can present in PACU, and rising temp, hypercarbia, tachycardia, and rigidity call for immediate treatment with dantrolene. The distractors treat symptoms only.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients should have postop glucose checked?
options: Patients on insulin infusions in the ICU
Patients with diabetes or glucose risk
questions.explanation: Pre and postop glucose checks should be ordered and documented for patients at risk, such as those with diabetes. Limiting checks to insulin infusions or children misses at-risk patients.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patients need postoperative electrolyte attention in PACU? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Renal disease, especially dialysis, and thyroid or parathyroid surgery (calcium) need electrolyte attention. Minor procedures don't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after total thyroidectomy reports perioral tingling and has a positive Chvostek sign. Which electrolyte is MOST likely abnormal?
questions.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid injury or removal causes hypocalcemia, with perioral numbness and Chvostek sign. The other electrolytes aren't typical.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which situations make acid-base disturbances more likely in PACU? (Select 4)
options: Healthy patient after a hand block
questions.explanation: High blood loss, mass transfusion, pulmonary disease, and renal disease raise acid-base risk. Minor procedures don't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which patient-related factors are traditional cardiovascular risk factors after noncardiac surgery?
options: Young age, female sex, and nonsmoking status
questions.explanation: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and current smoking are traditional patient risk factors. The others aren't.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which surgery types had the highest incidence of death or MI after noncardiac surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Thoracic, vascular, general, and neurosurgery had the highest incidence. Eye and skin procedures are low risk.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Which measures help minimize postoperative myocardial ischemia? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Continued beta blockers, analgesia, nitrates, oxygen, adequate volume and oxygen-carrying capacity, HR control, and attention to hypercoagulability help. Nitrates are among the listed measures.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: High-risk vascular patient in PACU has new ST depression. What monitoring approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Wait for chest pain before ordering any testing
questions.explanation: 5-lead ST monitoring, ECGs, and biomarkers detect ischemia, ideally compared with preop baselines. Many perioperative MIs are silent.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: Why are preop ECG, BNP, and cardiac enzymes useful in high-risk patients?
questions.explanation: Baseline values allow comparison when postop ischemia is suspected. They don't predict PONV or replace monitoring and aren't needed for every patient.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient with CAD has BP 196/104 and HR 118, SpO2 96%, normal EtCO2, and pain 7/10. What is the BEST approach?
options: Give a 1 L fluid bolus before treating the pain
Treat pain, then control BP and HR if needed
questions.explanation: After ruling out hypoxemia and hypercarbia, pain treatment often resolves hypertension and tachycardia; remaining elevation needs pharmacologic control, especially with CAD. Rate control alone ignores pain.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient becomes acutely tachycardic (HR 135), hypotensive (BP 82/50), and hypoxemic after hip replacement. Breath sounds are equal. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Tachycardia with hypotension and hypoxemia after orthopedic surgery suggests thromboembolism or fat embolism. Pain, anxiety, and bladder distension cause hypertension rather than hypotension.

sourceMeta.sourcePackage: PACU and Ambulatory / Office-Based Anesthesia: 500-Question Bank

questions.stem: PACU patient after central line placement develops tachycardia, hypotension, absent breath sounds on the right, and tracheal deviation. What is the BEST step?
options: Needle decompression of the right chest
Chest X-ray before any treatment is started
questions.explanation: These findings suggest tension pneumothorax, which needs immediate decompression. Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving care.
